title: AppHost 7 - Phase 0
subtitle: PROJ-824 - the phase 0 plan, step by step, for approval.
idea: Phase 0 builds the road, not the houses: we measure today, test the risky parts, and build the new pieces switched off, so clients see no change.

hero_visual.caption: Every new piece ships switched off until the go decision.

decision: Approve phase 0, then fill in the answer sheet after step 12.
opening: Phase 0 prepares the move to AppHost 7.
It builds the process and the tools, not real screens.
The Holiday screens in phase 1 are the first real test.
Clients see no change, because every new piece stays switched off.
The work uses spare developer hours, not paid client hours.

steps.name: Checks A to K
steps.sub: on the test server, A and B first
steps.lead: These 11 small experiments test the risky assumptions before any real screen is built.
steps.analogy: Before building a bridge, engineers drill test holes. A bad hole changes the plan cheaply, before any steel goes up.

note.title: Run first
note.text: A and B run first, because a failure there changes the stack and the back-end plan.

head: Check
What we try
Why it matters
rows: A
A test .NET 10 program calls one real VB6 component and times many calls at once.
The whole plan assumes new code can call the old components.
B
The same program calls one AppHostAPI function.
If it fails, AppHostAPI screens wait for a later phase.
C
Find out how the old components are hosted.
It decides whether the new service must run as 32-bit.
D
The web server runs a test React page and a test .NET service next to AppHost.
It proves the new pieces can live beside AppHost.
E
Check the AppHost login cookie's safety flags and whether the new service can read it.
The prototype reuses today's login.
F
Try the router option chosen in question 3.
The router sends users to old or new screens.
G
Find money calculations in old pages and test expired sessions in stored procedures.
New code must round money the same way and keep session checks.
H
List every way into each page: menu, links, redirects, form posts and bookmarks.
A menu-only router misses the other ways in.
I
Flip a test switch and time how long running pages take to see it.
AppHost keeps settings in memory, so a flip may lag.
J
Record today's page load times.
It gives a speed baseline for the extra hop to the new service.
K
Ask clients which browsers they use, and make a scrubbed test copy of the database.
Bank desktops may pin old browsers, and tests never use live client data.

note.title: Shared server
note.text: The test server is shared with QA, so we look first, back up, and ask before any change.

check.q: Why do checks A and B go first?
check.a: If new code cannot call the old VB6 or AppHostAPI code, the stack and back-end plan change.

steps.takeaway: Cheap experiments now prevent expensive surprises later.

steps.name: Stack and starter
steps.lead: We confirm the tools, then prove them with one throwaway screen.

bullets: Recommended stack: React + Vite for screens and C# on .NET LTS for the back-end service.
Other options on the table: Next.js, htmx + Razor, Blazor or Angular.
Checks A to D must pass before the stack is confirmed.
Acme sets the direction in [question 4](#q4).

head: Option
Pros
Cons
rows: React + Vite
React rarely ships a major version and backports security fixes. Plain files on IIS, so nothing new on client servers. The developer knows React.
We pick and maintain our own add-on libraries.
Next.js
The other Acme team's standard. Built on React, so skills transfer.
Each major version is supported 2 years, with a new one yearly. Its server parts need Node.js on every client server.
htmx + Razor
One language, C#. Few upgrades. Closest to today's pages.
Less suited to live, app-like screens. Less reuse of React skills.
Blazor
One language, C#. Ships with .NET.
Upgrades every 2 years with .NET. Fewer developers know it.
Angular
Full framework. The developer has some experience.
Each major version is supported 24 months, with a new one yearly.

note.text: The React, UX and .NET experts should review this table before the stack is final.

steps.name: Strangler Fig recipe
steps.lead: The recipe is the fixed set of steps that moves one screen from old to new.
steps.analogy: A strangler fig is a vine that grows around a tree until it replaces it. The new AppHost grows around the old one, one feature at a time.

bullets: In software, the new system grows around the old one, one feature at a time.
The old system keeps working the whole time.
Every click passes through one front door, the router.
The router reads one switch per feature in System Settings.

svg_file.caption: Old and new run side by side. System Settings decides per feature, and switching back loses no data.

head: Stage
What the router does
rows: Today
Every switch says old, so every click goes to the old pages.
During the work
Converted features go to new screens, and the rest stay old.
The end
Every switch says new, and the old pages can be switched off.

numbered: Add the feature's switch in System Settings, set to old.
Build the new screen with the starter project.
Call old components only through one adapter.
Run a parity test against the old page.
Add the router entry for the feature.
Turn the switch on for Acme staff, then one user group, then the whole client.
Delete the old page when the written rule says it is safe.

check.q: What happens to data if a switch is flipped back to old?
check.a: Nothing is lost. Old and new save through the same stored procedures.

steps.takeaway: New grows around old, one switch at a time, and either side can take the next click.

steps.name: Router
steps.lead: The router is the front door that sends each click to the old page or the new screen.
steps.analogy: Think of a railway switch. Flipping the lever sends the next train down the other track, and no track is torn up.

bullets: We build the router option Acme picks in [question 3](#q3).
Every switch starts off, so clients see no change.
We prove it with the dummy screen at all three switch levels.
Check H must find every way into a page, not only the menu.

chips: Next click goes the new way
Flip back: next click goes old

bullets: The switch can be on for Acme staff, one user group, or a whole client.
Once the setting reloads, the next click goes the new way, with no install.
No data moves, because both sides save through the same stored procedures.
Check I measures how long the reload takes.

check.q: Does turning a screen on need an install?
check.a: No. An admin flips its switch in System Settings, and the next click goes the new way once the setting reloads.

steps.takeaway: One switch per feature, flipped in settings, decides old or new for the next click.

steps.name: Security and session
steps.lead: The new service needs a written security design before any real screen uses it.

bullets: The security expert writes the security design of the new service.

head: Concern
Why it matters
rows: Today's login cookie has known weak spots.
Users can change cookie values that the server trusts.
Any new session must keep the SessionData row.
Many stored procedures record the session ID for audit.
A login token must never sit in browser storage.
A script on the page could steal it.

after: Move to login tokens such as JWT through one adapter.

steps.takeaway: Security is designed and written down before any real screen depends on it.

glossary: Strangler Fig
Replace an old system one feature at a time while old and new run side by side.
Router
The piece that sends each user to the old page or the new screen.
Switch
An on/off setting in System Settings that the router reads per feature.
Switch levels
A switch can be on for Acme staff, one user group, or a whole client.
Holiday prototype
The market-holiday calendar screens, the first real screens to convert.
Dummy screen
A throwaway test screen that proves the new pieces work together.
React + Vite
The recommended tools for building new screens in the browser.
.NET LTS
Microsoft's long-term-support release, the recommended base for the new service.
VB6 components
The old business-logic programs that AppHost pages call today.
AppHostAPI
AppHost's existing .NET 4.8 bridge to outside systems.
Adapter
One small wrapper, so new code calls an old component in one place only.
Parity test
Proof that a new screen shows the same data as the old page.
Session
The record that a user is logged in, stored in the SessionData table.
JWT
A signed login token, one option for a stronger session.
Screen factory
A repeatable line where a skill picks the next page, Claude drafts it, and review skills and a person check it.
Triage skill
An AI instruction set that reads the Jira board and picks the next page to convert.
Review skill
An AI reviewer that checks each change against one member's written standards.
Eval
A set of planted mistakes that a review skill must catch.
Merge request
A proposed code change that is reviewed before it joins the main code.
Bond screens
The variable-rate bond screens in AppHost.
PROJ-824 sheet
The Google sheet that lists every AppHost screen, report, batch job and helper file.
IIS
Microsoft's web server, which runs AppHost's pages at each client.
Stored procedure
A saved SQL program in the database that both old and new code call.
